questions.subject: History
questions.text: The theory that the Yoruba originated from a migration led by Oduduwa from the east is commonly known as the
options: Bayajidda legend
Hamitic hypothesis
Oduduwa migration theory of Yoruba origin
autochthonous (indigenous) theory of Yoruba origin
questions.explanation: One major tradition of Yoruba origin holds that Oduduwa led a migration from the east and settled at Ile-Ife, from where his descendants founded the various Yoruba kingdoms.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Bayajidda legend is a foundation myth most closely associated with the origin of the
options: Hausa states
Kanem-Bornu Empire
Yoruba kingdoms
Benin Kingdom
questions.explanation: The Bayajidda legend, involving a heroic stranger who slays a snake in a well at Daura, is the traditional account explaining the founding of the seven true Hausa states (Hausa Bakwai).

questions.subject: History
questions.text: In traditional Benin political history, the transition from the Ogiso dynasty to the Oba dynasty is closely linked to the invitation extended to a prince from
options: Kano
Ile-Ife
Old Oyo
Sokoto
questions.explanation: Benin oral tradition holds that after the Ogiso dynasty ended, Benin chiefs invited a prince (Oranmiyan) from Ile-Ife, whose son Eweka I became the first Oba, beginning the present dynasty.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of these describes the general system of land tenure practised in most pre-colonial Nigerian societies before 1800?
options: Land ownership was determined solely by written colonial title deeds
Land was generally held communally by families, lineages, or the community, rather than owned by individuals
All land belonged exclusively to foreign trading companies
Land was bought and sold freely on an open individual market
questions.explanation: Across most pre-colonial Nigerian societies, land was typically held in trust by families, lineages, or communities under customary law, rather than being individually owned property.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The nine-mile-long defensive earthwork known as the Sungbo's Eredo is associated with which pre-colonial Nigerian kingdom?
options: The Kano Emirate
The Ijebu Kingdom
The Kwararafa Kingdom
The Benin Kingdom
questions.explanation: Sungbo's Eredo is a massive system of walls and ditches associated with the Ijebu Kingdom, believed to have been constructed for defensive and boundary purposes.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The extensive system of earthworks and moats surrounding Benin City, among the largest man-made structures in pre-colonial Africa, primarily served the purpose of
options: channelling water for large-scale irrigation farming
defending the kingdom and demarcating its boundaries
housing the kingdom's bronze-casting guilds
storing surplus agricultural produce
questions.explanation: The Benin Walls and moats were built over centuries chiefly for defence against invasion and to mark out the boundaries of the expanding kingdom and its subordinate settlements.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Among the Igbo, the title-taking system such as Ozo was significant mainly because it
options: was reserved exclusively for hereditary monarchs
conferred status and authority on individuals based on achievement rather than inherited kingship
replaced all forms of village council government
was introduced by British colonial administrators
questions.explanation: In the largely decentralised Igbo political system, title systems like Ozo allowed individuals to earn social prestige and influence through personal achievement, wealth, and initiation, rather than through inherited kingship.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nupe Kingdom, located in the Niger-Benue confluence area, was historically ruled by a monarch bearing the title of
options: Etsu Nupe
Obi of Onitsha
Attah of Igala
Amanyanabo
questions.explanation: The Nupe Kingdom's traditional ruler held the title Etsu Nupe, governing from centres such as Bida in the pre-colonial and later emirate period.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: In the pre-1800 Niger Delta city-states, the office of the 'Amanyanabo' referred to the
options: commander of an Oyo cavalry regiment
senior priest responsible for oracle consultations
head or king of a Delta trading state such as Bonny or Kalabari
leader of a Benin-appointed provincial administration
questions.explanation: 'Amanyanabo', meaning 'owner of the land', was the title used for the ruling head of several Niger Delta city-states engaged in coastal and overseas trade.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A key economic factor that encouraged the rise of centralised states such as Old Oyo and Benin in the forest belt was
options: control of long-distance trade routes linking the coast, the forest, and the savanna
an economy based purely on nomadic pastoralism
reliance on a single crop with no trading surplus
the total absence of any trade with neighbouring peoples
questions.explanation: States like Old Oyo and Benin grew powerful partly by controlling and taxing trade routes connecting northern savanna markets, forest producers, and the Atlantic coast.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Islam was introduced into Hausaland mainly through the influence of
options: the trans-Atlantic slave trade
Portuguese explorers along the coast
direct British colonial missionary activity
Wangarawa (Mande-speaking) traders and clerics from the western Sudan
questions.explanation: Islam spread into Hausaland from around the 14th century largely through Wangarawa traders and Muslim clerics travelling from the western Sudanic empires, well before any European contact.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Before the 19th-century Jihad, Hausa society was already marked by a degree of religious tension mainly between
options: Buddhist and Hindu trading communities
Roman Catholic and Protestant Christian communities
Islamic practice among the ruling and merchant classes and persistent traditional (Maguzawa) religious practices among much of the peasantry
Sunni and Shia populations of equal size
questions.explanation: Although Islam had taken root among Hausa rulers and traders, many rural Hausa (the Maguzawa) retained traditional religious practices, a tension Uthman Dan Fodio later cited as justification for reform.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The trans-Saharan trade that flourished across the Nigeria area before 1800 principally exchanged North African goods such as salt and cloth for southern products including
options: gold, kola nuts, leather, and slaves
crude oil and timber
maize and cassava
cocoa and rubber
questions.explanation: Trans-Saharan caravans typically carried salt, cloth, and horses southward, returning north with gold, kola nuts, leather goods, and enslaved people obtained from the savanna and forest zones.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best explains why many Igbo communities in the pre-1800 period lacked centralised kingship, unlike Benin or Oyo?
options: British colonial policy had already abolished Igbo kingship by that period
They had no contact whatsoever with neighbouring centralised states
They were entirely nomadic and therefore could not sustain fixed institutions
Their political system emphasised village democracy through councils of elders, age grades, and title societies
questions.explanation: Most pre-colonial Igbo communities practised a form of village-based, republican governance relying on councils of elders, age grades, and title societies rather than a single centralised monarch.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Uthman Dan Fodio's Jihad formally began in 1804 at
options: Kano, the largest Hausa city
Sokoto, already established as the caliphate's capital
Gudu, where he made the hijra (withdrawal) and was declared Amir al-Mu'minin
Ilorin, a Yoruba frontier town
questions.explanation: In 1804, Dan Fodio withdrew (hijra) to Gudu with his followers, where he was proclaimed Amir al-Mu'minin (Commander of the Faithful), marking the formal start of the Jihad.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Within the Sokoto Caliphate's administrative structure, overall spiritual and political leadership was vested in the
options: Shehu of Bornu
Alaafin of Oyo
Sultan of Sokoto
Emir of Zaria alone, independent of Sokoto
questions.explanation: The Sultan of Sokoto stood at the apex of the Caliphate, exercising ultimate spiritual and political authority over the various emirates, which retained a degree of local autonomy under their Emirs.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Muhammed Bello, a key successor to Uthman Dan Fodio, is particularly remembered for
options: founding the city-state of Ibadan
leading the original 1804 Jihad from its start
signing the earliest treaty with British colonial officials
consolidating and administering the Sokoto Caliphate after the Jihad, and founding Sokoto as its capital
questions.explanation: Muhammed Bello, Dan Fodio's son, succeeded him as Caliph, founded Sokoto as the new capital, and played a central role in consolidating and administering the vast Caliphate.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Unlike Hausaland, the Kanem-Bornu Empire successfully resisted absorption into the Sokoto Caliphate largely due to the leadership of
options: Uthman Dan Fodio himself, who chose to spare Bornu
British colonial forces who intervened to protect Bornu
the Alaafin of Oyo, who allied with Bornu against Sokoto
Muhammad al-Kanemi, who reorganised Bornu's defences and religious authority
questions.explanation: Muhammad al-Kanemi rallied Bornu's forces and religious scholarship to repel Fulani Jihadist advances, preserving Bornu's independence and eventually founding a new ruling dynasty there.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Fulani Jihadists' establishment of the Ilorin Emirate in Yorubaland is closely linked to the actions of
options: the Oyomesi council, seeking to strengthen the Alaafin's authority
British colonial officers seeking a buffer state
Muhammed Bello, acting entirely without local Yoruba involvement
Afonja, the Are-Ona-Kakanfo, who invited Fulani support against the Alaafin
questions.explanation: Afonja, the Oyo military commander at Ilorin, rebelled against the Alaafin and enlisted Fulani and Hausa support; this alliance eventually resulted in Ilorin becoming a Fulani-ruled emirate.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The founding of Ibadan as a major 19th-century Yoruba power is best explained by its origins as a
options: religious centre founded by Fulani clerics
colonial administrative headquarters created by the British
war camp that grew into a powerful city-state through military success in the Yoruba civil wars
trading post established directly by European merchants
questions.explanation: Ibadan began as a war camp of refugees and warriors from various Yoruba towns and rose to prominence through military strength during the chaotic period of the Yoruba civil wars.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Kiriji War (Ekiti-Parapo War) of the late 19th century was fought mainly between
options: Benin and the Itsekiri
the Sokoto Caliphate and Bornu
Ibadan and an alliance of Ekiti, Ijesa, and other Yoruba groups
British forces and the Ijebu
questions.explanation: The prolonged Kiriji War pitted Ibadan against the Ekitiparapo alliance (Ekiti, Ijesa, and others), representing one of the longest and most destructive conflicts of the Yoruba civil war era.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Kiriji War was eventually brought to an end largely through
options: direct intervention by the Sokoto Caliphate
a decision of the Oyomesi council of Old Oyo
Ibadan's total military conquest of all opposing forces
British mediation, which led to a peace treaty in 1886
questions.explanation: British officials, keen to secure stability for trade, mediated between the warring Yoruba factions, contributing to the peace agreement that ended the Kiriji War in 1886.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Following the collapse of Old Oyo, the Alaafin's court and remaining Oyo authority relocated southward and was eventually re-established at
options: Abeokuta
New Oyo (Ago-Oja)
Ijebu-Ode
Ibadan
questions.explanation: After the destruction of the old capital, the Oyo court moved and was eventually resettled at Ago-Oja, which became known as New Oyo, though with much reduced power compared to the old empire.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The founding of Abeokuta in the 1830s is best explained as a
options: new capital deliberately established by the Sokoto Caliphate
colonial town created directly by British administrators
trading post founded solely by Portuguese merchants
refuge settlement created by Egba groups displaced by the Yoruba civil wars
questions.explanation: Abeokuta was founded as a fortified refuge ('under the rock') by Egba communities fleeing the instability and warfare that followed the collapse of Old Oyo.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 19th-century Nupe Kingdom came under Fulani rule largely as a result of
options: a peaceful dynastic marriage alliance
direct British colonial conquest
the intervention of the Alaafin of Oyo
a Jihadist takeover led by Mallam Dendo and his successors
questions.explanation: Mallam Dendo, a Fulani cleric, exploited a succession dispute in the Nupe Kingdom to establish Fulani political dominance, eventually founding a new emirate dynasty at Bida.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A major long-term political consequence of the 19th-century upheavals (the Sokoto Jihad and the Yoruba civil wars) was that
options: the region achieved complete and lasting political unity
the trans-Atlantic slave trade was permanently ended within the region
Nigeria's pre-colonial political landscape was significantly reshaped just before the onset of British colonial rule
European contact with the interior ceased entirely
questions.explanation: The dramatic 19th-century transformations — the rise of the Sokoto Caliphate and the fragmentation of Yorubaland — reshaped the political map of the Nigeria area on the very eve of British colonisation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 19th-century Jihad and subsequent wars in the Nigeria area contributed to an increase in the internal (domestic) slave trade mainly because
options: slavery had been completely unknown before this period
all captives were immediately freed under Islamic law
large numbers of war captives were enslaved and put to use within African societies, including on plantations
the British actively encouraged internal enslavement during this period
questions.explanation: The extensive warfare of the Jihad and the Yoruba civil wars generated large numbers of captives, many of whom were enslaved and used domestically, including on the plantations that emerged around this period.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following Yoruba towns is most closely associated with serving as a key middleman trading centre between the interior and European traders on the coast during the 19th century?
options: Sokoto
Bornu
Ijebu-Ode
Kano
questions.explanation: Ijebu-Ode occupied a strategic position between the Yoruba interior and the coast, and the Ijebu long controlled and profited from trade passing through their territory to European merchants.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Lagos was formally annexed by the British in
questions.explanation: Lagos was annexed as a British colony in 1861, decades before the wider amalgamation of Nigeria, largely to suppress the slave trade and secure British commercial interests.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Royal Niger Company, chartered in 1886, was primarily significant for
options: granting Nigeria's independence
leading the Sokoto Jihad
administering and controlling trade in the Niger area under a British royal charter before direct colonial rule was established
organising the Berlin Conference
questions.explanation: Under Sir George Goldie, the Royal Niger Company held a royal charter to trade and administer territory along the Niger, effectively laying groundwork for later formal British colonial control.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The British Protectorate of Southern Nigeria and the Protectorate of Northern Nigeria were formally proclaimed in
questions.explanation: In 1900, the British Crown took over administration from the Royal Niger Company, formally establishing the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria ahead of the 1914 amalgamation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The British conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate was effectively completed with the fall of the city of
options: Zaria in 1908
Ilorin in 1897
Kano in 1914
Sokoto itself in 1903
questions.explanation: British forces under Frederick Lugard captured Sokoto in 1903, marking the effective end of the Caliphate's independent political and military authority.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The British conquest of the Benin Kingdom in 1897 was triggered directly by
options: a formal declaration of war by the Oba against Britain
a boundary dispute between Benin and Lagos
the killing of members of a British trade delegation, prompting a punitive expedition
an uprising among Benin's own chiefs against the Oba
questions.explanation: After a British-led delegation was attacked and several members killed near Benin, Britain launched a large punitive expedition in 1897 that captured and looted Benin City.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A major consequence of the 1897 Punitive Expedition against Benin was
options: the immediate granting of self-rule to Benin
the peaceful integration of Benin as an equal partner in colonial government
the exile of Oba Ovonramwen and the seizure of thousands of Benin artworks, including the Benin Bronzes
the establishment of Benin as the colonial capital of Southern Nigeria
questions.explanation: Following the expedition, Oba Ovonramwen was deposed and exiled, and British forces looted a vast quantity of Benin's royal art, much of which remains in foreign museums today.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Indirect Rule faced its greatest practical difficulty in Eastern Nigeria mainly because
options: the region had no economic resources of interest to Britain
many Igbo communities lacked the centralised, hereditary chieftaincy structures the system assumed
the Igbo had no contact whatsoever with the colonial government
Eastern Nigeria had already gained self-government before 1900
questions.explanation: Because Indirect Rule was modelled on the emirate system, its imposition on the largely decentralised Igbo areas required artificial 'warrant chiefs', which lacked genuine traditional legitimacy.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Colonial 'pacification' campaigns in the Nigeria area referred to
options: peaceful diplomatic negotiations that avoided all use of force
campaigns run by missionaries with no military involvement
military expeditions used by the British to subdue resistant communities and extend colonial control
programmes to end domestic conflicts between rival Nigerian ethnic groups after independence
questions.explanation: 'Pacification' was the term colonial authorities used for military campaigns aimed at forcibly subduing resistant communities and consolidating British administrative control over new territories.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Anglo-Aro War (1901-1902) was fought by the British mainly to break the power of
options: the Ijebu Kingdom
the Sokoto Caliphate
the Aro Confederacy and its Long Juju oracle network in the Igbo hinterland
the Benin Kingdom
questions.explanation: The Aro Confederacy exercised extensive religious and commercial influence, notably through the Ibinukpabi (Long Juju) oracle; the British campaign aimed to dismantle this network and extend colonial control.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The British defeat of the Ijebu Kingdom in 1892 was significant chiefly because it
options: occurred without any resistance from Ijebu forces
led immediately to full Nigerian independence
marked the final British military campaign in Nigeria
opened up the Yoruba interior to more direct British commercial and political penetration
questions.explanation: The Ijebu had long acted as middlemen restricting British access to the interior; their defeat in 1892 removed this barrier and accelerated British commercial and political expansion into Yorubaland.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nana Olomu of Itsekiri resistance against British commercial encroachment in the late 19th century was fundamentally a dispute over
options: control of the palm oil trade and middleman trading privileges in the Niger Delta
religious differences between Christianity and traditional beliefs
control of the Sokoto Caliphate's northern trade routes
the right to appoint the Oba of Benin
questions.explanation: Nana Olomu, a powerful Itsekiri trading chief, resisted British efforts to bypass African middlemen and trade directly in the interior, particularly over lucrative palm oil trade.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: King Jaja of Opobo's resistance to British trading interests in the 1880s ultimately resulted in his
options: arrest and exile by the British
alliance with the Sokoto Caliphate against Britain
formal recognition as a British colonial governor
successful expulsion of all British traders from the Niger Delta
questions.explanation: King Jaja of Opobo, who sought to control his own trade with Europe rather than accept British middlemen restrictions, was lured aboard a British ship, arrested, and exiled to the West Indies.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Colonial direct taxation, a recurring trigger of resistance movements such as the Adubi War and the Aba Women's Riot, was resented largely because it
options: applied exclusively to European residents in Nigeria
was seen as an unprecedented imposition that undermined existing customary obligations and economic autonomy
had already existed in identical form under pre-colonial rulers
was welcomed unanimously by all Nigerian communities
questions.explanation: In many areas, direct colonial taxation represented a novel and unwelcome imposition that clashed with existing customary economic arrangements, generating widespread resentment and, at times, open resistance.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The colonial policy of using warrant chiefs in Igboland is best described as an attempt to
options: replace Islamic emirate rulers in the North
abolish all forms of local government entirely
create artificial local authorities where none of the required kind previously existed, to serve Indirect Rule
restore the exact powers of pre-existing Igbo kings
questions.explanation: Since Indirect Rule required identifiable local rulers, the British appointed warrant chiefs in many Igbo communities that traditionally had no single hereditary ruler, often provoking resentment due to their lack of legitimacy.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best captures the overall economic relationship established between colonial Nigeria and Britain?
options: Britain provided Nigeria with the majority of its food imports
Nigeria's economy was entirely self-contained and had no trade links with Britain
Nigeria mainly supplied raw materials and cash crops while importing British manufactured goods
Nigeria and Britain traded as economic equals with balanced industrial exchange
questions.explanation: Colonial economic policy structured Nigeria's economy around the export of raw materials and cash crops to Britain, in exchange for imported British manufactured goods, a classic colonial trade pattern.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The West African Students' Union (WASU), founded in London in 1925, played an important role in Nigerian nationalism mainly by
options: negotiating the Berlin Conference agreements
organising Nigeria's first general election
fostering pan-African political consciousness among Nigerian and other West African students studying abroad
administering the Sokoto Caliphate
questions.explanation: WASU brought together West African students in Britain, exposing many future Nigerian nationalist leaders to pan-African ideas and political organisation that shaped later independence movements.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nigerian Youth Movement (NYM), formed in the 1930s, is significant as one of the first Nigerian nationalist organisations to
options: openly reject any form of Nigerian self-government
attract broad-based, cross-regional membership demanding greater Nigerian self-government
restrict its membership exclusively to Northern Nigeria
be founded directly by the British colonial government
questions.explanation: The NYM drew members from various regions and backgrounds, marking an important step toward broader nationalist mobilisation beyond earlier, more localised political associations.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Obafemi Awolowo's early political career included founding the pan-Yoruba cultural and political organisation known as
options: Egbe Omo Oduduwa
the Sokoto Council
the Nigerian Youth Movement
the Northern People's Congress
questions.explanation: Awolowo founded Egbe Omo Oduduwa in 1948 as a pan-Yoruba cultural organisation, which later provided much of the political base for the Action Group.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Northern Elements Progressive Union (NEPU), led by figures such as Aminu Kano, distinguished itself from the NPC mainly by
options: opposing any form of Nigerian independence
advocating radical social reform and challenging the traditional emirate ruling establishment in the North
supporting the continuation of British colonial rule indefinitely
restricting its activities to Southern Nigeria
questions.explanation: NEPU, associated with Aminu Kano, took a more radical, reformist stance than the NPC, criticising the conservative emirate establishment and calling for greater social and political change in the North.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1953 Kano Riots were significantly triggered by
options: disagreements over the location of Nigeria's new capital
the outcome of Nigeria's independence referendum
a dispute over colonial taxation policy
political and ethnic tensions arising from a heated debate over the timing of Nigerian self-government
questions.explanation: The 1953 Kano riots followed sharp regional and ethnic tensions after Southern-based politicians pushed for an early date for Nigerian self-government, a proposal Northern leaders resisted.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1957 and 1958 Constitutional Conferences held in London were mainly concerned with
options: establishing the Nigerian Civil War peace terms
abolishing the regional system of government
declaring Nigeria's independence immediately
resolving outstanding constitutional issues, including minority concerns, ahead of Nigerian independence
questions.explanation: These London conferences addressed key unresolved issues, including the fears of ethnic minorities within the regions, as part of the process of finalising arrangements for Nigerian independence.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Willink Commission of 1957-1958 was established mainly to investigate
options: the effectiveness of Indirect Rule in Northern Nigeria
the fears of ethnic minorities and consider possible safeguards, including the question of separate states
the terms of the Berlin Conference
the causes of the Nigerian Civil War
questions.explanation: The Willink Commission was set up by the British government to examine the concerns of minority ethnic groups within Nigeria's three regions and recommend safeguards ahead of independence.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: At the 1960 independence, Nnamdi Azikiwe assumed the position of
options: Premier of the Western Region
first Prime Minister of Nigeria
Premier of the Northern Region
Governor-General, and later the first President when Nigeria became a republic in 1963
questions.explanation: Azikiwe became Nigeria's first indigenous Governor-General at independence in 1960, and subsequently the first President when Nigeria adopted a republican constitution in 1963.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa's role at the time of Nigeria's 1960 independence was that of
options: President of the Senate
Premier of the Eastern Region
Prime Minister, heading the federal government
Governor-General
questions.explanation: Tafawa Balewa served as Nigeria's first Prime Minister, leading the federal government under the parliamentary system established at independence in 1960.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: A key demand shared broadly by Nigerian nationalist movements across regions in the years before independence was
options: abolition of the regional system rather than any form of self-rule
the permanent retention of British colonial administration
an accelerated timetable for full self-government and eventual independence from British rule
closer political union with other British West African colonies as a single country
questions.explanation: Despite regional and ideological differences, Nigerian nationalist parties broadly agreed on pressing for a faster path to self-government and full independence from Britain.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1959 Federal Election, held ahead of independence, is significant mainly because it
options: was cancelled due to widespread unrest
was Nigeria's first ever election of any kind
led directly to Nigeria becoming a republic
determined which coalition of parties would form Nigeria's first independent government
questions.explanation: The 1959 federal election results led to a coalition government between the NPC and NCNC, which formed Nigeria's government at the point of independence in October 1960.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Compared to the NCNC and Action Group, the Northern People's Congress (NPC) in the pre-independence period is generally described as
options: a party founded and led primarily by Southern politicians
more cautious about rapid self-government, prioritising Northern regional interests and gradual change
the most radical party demanding immediate independence
opposed in principle to any Nigerian self-government
questions.explanation: The NPC, closely tied to the Northern emirate establishment, generally favoured a more gradual approach to self-government, wary that rapid change might disadvantage the North relative to the more educationally advanced South.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The transformation of Nigeria's colonial constitutional structure from unitary control toward federalism was primarily driven by
options: the need to accommodate Nigeria's ethnic, regional, and cultural diversity
pressure from other independent African states
a direct instruction from the League of Nations
the outcome of the Nigerian Civil War
questions.explanation: Nigeria's shift toward a federal structure, beginning with the Richards Constitution, reflected the practical need to manage the country's considerable ethnic, cultural, and regional diversity.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The role of the press, such as Azikiwe's West African Pilot, in the Nigerian independence movement was mainly to
options: focus exclusively on sports and entertainment news
serve as an official mouthpiece of the colonial government
mobilise public opinion and criticise colonial policies in support of nationalist goals
avoid any discussion of political matters
questions.explanation: Nationalist-owned newspapers such as the West African Pilot played an active role in shaping public opinion, criticising colonial policy, and rallying support for self-government.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following best explains the choice of a federal, rather than unitary, system of government for independent Nigeria in 1960?
options: It offered a practical means of balancing regional autonomy with national unity across a diverse country
It eliminated the need for any central government institutions
It was a system copied directly from the government of ancient Songhai
It was imposed without consultation by the United Nations
questions.explanation: Federalism was adopted as a pragmatic compromise, allowing regions considerable autonomy over local affairs while preserving a unified central government for a country with wide ethnic and regional diversity.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The controversial national population census of 1962/1963 contributed to post-independence tension mainly because
options: it was conducted entirely by foreign observers with no local input
it was Nigeria's first ever census under any government
it revealed there was no ethnic diversity in Nigeria
its results were disputed and seen as tied to regional political and resource-allocation advantage
questions.explanation: Because population figures affected regional representation and revenue allocation, the disputed 1962/1963 census results heightened regional and political rivalries in the early 1960s.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Western Region crisis of 1962, involving a split within the Action Group, most directly resulted in
options: the creation of the Mid-Western Region
Nigeria's first military coup
a state of emergency being declared in the Western Region
the outbreak of the Nigerian Civil War
questions.explanation: Political conflict between Awolowo and Akintola factions within the Action Group led to serious unrest in the Western Region, prompting the federal government to declare a state of emergency there in 1962.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Mid-Western Region was created in 1963, becoming Nigeria's
options: first region created after independence
only region created through a military decree
final region before the Civil War, carved from the North
fourth region, carved mainly out of the former Western Region
questions.explanation: The Mid-Western Region was created in 1963 out of parts of the Western Region, becoming the fourth of Nigeria's regions and addressing some minority demands in the area.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 'Operation Wetie' unrest that followed the disputed Western Region election of 1965 significantly contributed to
options: a breakdown of public order that helped precipitate the January 1966 military coup
the peaceful resolution of Nigeria's regional political disputes
the immediate return of Nigeria to a unitary system of government
the end of the Nigerian Civil War
questions.explanation: Widespread violence and arson ('Operation Wetie') following the contested 1965 Western Region election deepened the political crisis that set the stage for the military takeover in January 1966.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Yakubu Gowon's decision to create 12 states out of the four regions in 1967 was announced
options: shortly before the outbreak of the Nigerian Civil War, partly to undercut support for Biafran secession
immediately after the end of the Nigerian Civil War
at the moment of Nigeria's 1960 independence
during the Second Republic under President Shagari
questions.explanation: Gowon's 12-state creation in May 1967 was announced just before the Civil War began, aiming partly to weaken support for Eastern Region secession by addressing minority grievances within the region.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Nigerian Civil War is generally understood to have been fuelled in part by economic considerations related to control of
options: cocoa plantations in the West
gold deposits in Northern Nigeria
newly discovered oil reserves located mainly within the Eastern Region
salt mines in the Sahara-facing north
questions.explanation: The prospect of substantial oil revenue located largely within Eastern Nigeria was a significant economic factor underlying both the region's confidence in seceding and the federal government's determination to prevent it.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Murtala Mohammed, who came to power in a 1975 coup, is particularly remembered for
options: declaring Nigeria's independence in 1960
launching a vigorous programme to purge the civil service and prepare a transition to civilian rule
leading Nigeria into the Civil War
founding the Action Group political party
questions.explanation: Murtala Mohammed's short but energetic regime pursued reforms including a major civil service purge and set in motion a transition programme toward civilian rule, continued after his assassination by Olusegun Obasanjo.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 1979 Constitution, which ushered in Nigeria's Second Republic, marked a significant departure from the First Republic mainly by introducing a
options: return to a purely unitary system of government
one-party socialist state structure
continuation of the British parliamentary monarchy
presidential system of government modelled partly on that of the United States
questions.explanation: Unlike the parliamentary First Republic, the 1979 Constitution introduced a presidential system with an executive President, drawing significant inspiration from the American model.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Ibrahim Babangida's regime (1985-1993) is particularly remembered for its prolonged and ultimately incomplete transition programme, culminating in the annulment of the
options: 1959 federal election
1979 general election
1999 presidential election
12 June 1993 presidential election, widely believed to have been won by MKO Abiola
questions.explanation: Babangida's annulment of the June 12, 1993 election, generally regarded as Nigeria's freest and fairest at the time, triggered a severe political crisis and is widely seen as one of the darkest moments of Nigerian democratic history.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: General Sani Abacha's rule in the 1990s is widely associated with
options: the peaceful resolution of the June 12 crisis
a smooth and rapid transition to democratic government
intense authoritarian repression, including the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and other Ogoni activists
Nigeria's return to civilian rule in 1993
questions.explanation: Abacha's regime was marked by severe political repression, including the 1995 execution of environmental activist Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni leaders, drawing widespread international condemnation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Nigeria's Fourth Republic, beginning in 1999, is historically notable for representing
options: Nigeria's first ever attempt at civilian rule
the longest continuous period of civilian democratic governance in Nigeria's post-independence history
the final period before Nigeria's independence
a return to the parliamentary system used in the First Republic
questions.explanation: Since 1999, Nigeria has sustained an unbroken period of civilian democratic government, marking its longest such stretch since independence, despite the political challenges it has faced.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Revenue allocation has remained a persistent and contentious issue in post-independence Nigerian history mainly because of
options: the absence of any federal government structure
disagreements between the federal government and the states/regions over how to share national income, especially oil revenue
a complete lack of any natural resources within the country
unanimous agreement among all regions on a fixed permanent formula since 1960
questions.explanation: Since independence, the distribution of national revenue, particularly oil wealth, between the federal government and the constituent states has remained a recurring and often contentious political issue.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The creation of additional states beyond Gowon's original 12, continuing through subsequent military regimes, generally reflected ongoing
options: instructions from the United Nations Security Council
agreements reached at the Berlin Conference
attempts to abolish the federal system entirely
demands from various ethnic and local groups for greater self-administration and access to resources
questions.explanation: Successive rounds of state creation in Nigeria have generally responded to persistent local and ethnic demands for greater administrative autonomy and more direct access to resources and representation.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The transition from military to civilian rule in 1999 was significantly shaped by the sudden death of which military Head of State in mid-1998, which accelerated the transition process?
options: General Yakubu Gowon
General Ibrahim Babangida
General Sani Abacha
General Murtala Mohammed
questions.explanation: Abacha's sudden death in June 1998 led to General Abdulsalami Abubakar taking over and swiftly implementing a transition programme that culminated in the 1999 elections and the start of the Fourth Republic.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The West African empire of Ghana is generally believed to have declined significantly following invasions and pressure from the
options: Portuguese colonisers
Almoravids, a North African Berber Islamic movement
Mongol Empire
Ottoman Empire
questions.explanation: Historians commonly link the decline of ancient Ghana partly to military and religious pressure from the Almoravid movement in the 11th century, alongside internal weaknesses and the drying up of trade routes.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Following Mansa Musa's famous pilgrimage to Makkah, the Mali Empire's international reputation was significantly enhanced due to his
options: extravagant distribution of gold along the route, which drew wide attention to Mali's wealth
military conquest of Egypt
conversion of the entire Islamic world to traditional African religion
abolition of trade throughout West Africa
questions.explanation: Mansa Musa's lavish spending and gift-giving of gold during his pilgrimage caused a temporary devaluation of gold in some regions and dramatically raised international awareness of Mali's wealth.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The decline of the Mali Empire from the 15th century onward was significantly influenced by
options: a sudden and total loss of all gold resources
internal succession disputes and the rising power of the Songhai Empire
British colonial intervention
direct conquest by the Ottoman Empire
questions.explanation: Mali's decline resulted from a combination of internal political instability over succession and the growing military and political strength of the emerging Songhai Empire, which eventually eclipsed it.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The city of Jenne (Djenne), closely associated with the Mali and Songhai empires, was particularly renowned as a centre of
options: the trans-Atlantic slave trade
iron smelting technology unique to Southern Africa
Portuguese colonial administration
trade and Islamic scholarship, alongside Timbuktu
questions.explanation: Jenne, like Timbuktu, developed into a major centre of trade and Islamic learning in the Western Sudan, contributing significantly to the intellectual and commercial life of the Mali and Songhai empires.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The historic Kanem-Bornu Empire maintained diplomatic and religious contacts across the Sahara reaching as far as
options: the Ottoman Empire and North Africa
Western Europe directly, bypassing North Africa
the Kingdom of Portugal exclusively
the Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe
questions.explanation: Kanem-Bornu maintained active trans-Saharan diplomatic, religious, and commercial relations with North African states and, at times, the Ottoman Empire, reflecting its long-standing regional importance.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The prosperity of Great Zimbabwe, a major Southern African civilization, was built substantially on control of trade in
options: gold and ivory with the East African (Swahili) coast
kola nuts with the Guinea forest region
cocoa with European trading companies
salt with North African caravans
questions.explanation: Great Zimbabwe's wealth derived largely from its role in regional and long-distance trade, particularly the exchange of gold and ivory with Swahili coastal trading cities linked to the wider Indian Ocean trade.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The abolition of the trans-Atlantic slave trade by Britain in 1807 primarily affected West Africa by
options: gradually shifting British commercial interest toward 'legitimate' trade in goods such as palm oil
causing an instant and total collapse of West African economies
immediately ending all forms of slavery within Africa
leading directly to Nigeria's independence
questions.explanation: Following abolition, British commercial policy in West Africa gradually pivoted toward promoting 'legitimate' commerce, especially in commodities like palm oil, as a substitute for the slave trade.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Which of the following was a significant long-term social effect of the trans-Atlantic slave trade on West African societies?
options: Increased warfare and slave-raiding as some states sought captives to trade for European goods
The elimination of all forms of internal African trade
The immediate and complete disappearance of all indigenous political systems
Universal population growth across every affected region
questions.explanation: The demand for enslaved people to trade with Europeans encouraged increased warfare, raiding, and the militarisation of some African states seeking captives to exchange for firearms and other goods.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The European colonial power most associated with the policy of assimilation, distinct from the British approach of Indirect Rule, was
options: Belgium
Germany
Portugal
France
questions.explanation: French colonial policy, especially in West Africa, generally emphasised assimilation, aiming to culturally integrate colonial subjects into French civilisation, in contrast with the British preference for Indirect Rule.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: At the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, the principle used to justify a European power's claim to a given African territory generally required that power to demonstrate
options: a unanimous vote of all African leaders
effective occupation of the territory it claimed
religious conversion of the entire local population
prior ownership recognised by African rulers
questions.explanation: The Berlin Conference established the principle of 'effective occupation', requiring a European power to show genuine administrative or military presence to have its claim over African territory recognised by other powers.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Ethiopia's successful resistance to Italian colonisation at the Battle of Adwa in 1896 is historically significant because it
options: allowed Ethiopia to remain one of the very few African states to preserve its independence during the Scramble for Africa
led to the complete colonisation of the entire Horn of Africa by Italy
marked the beginning of the Scramble for Africa
was the first ever conflict between an African and a European power
questions.explanation: Ethiopia's decisive victory over Italy at Adwa in 1896 preserved its independence, making it (along with Liberia) one of the few African states to avoid European colonial rule during this period.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The 'legitimate trade' era in 19th-century West Africa refers to the period when European commerce shifted its focus mainly toward
options: the exclusive trade of gold and diamonds
agricultural and natural produce such as palm oil, groundnuts, and rubber, rather than enslaved people
arms trading with African military states
manufactured European textiles exclusively
questions.explanation: Following the decline of the slave trade, 'legitimate trade' centred on the export of agricultural and natural commodities like palm oil, groundnuts, and rubber to European markets.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Pan-Africanism, as an ideological and political movement, is best described as one that primarily promoted
options: solidarity, unity, and the liberation of African peoples and those of African descent worldwide
European control over African colonies in perpetuity
the division of Africa into smaller, competing ethnic states
exclusive economic ties between Africa and a single foreign power
questions.explanation: Pan-Africanism emerged as a movement advocating unity, solidarity, and eventual liberation for African peoples and the African diaspora, influencing independence movements across the continent, including in Nigeria.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: Kwame Nkrumah of Ghana is particularly significant in African history as
options: the founder of the ancient Mali Empire
a key leader of the Sokoto Jihad
the leader of the first Sub-Saharan African colony to achieve independence, in 1957
the ruler who built Great Zimbabwe
questions.explanation: Kwame Nkrumah led Ghana (the former Gold Coast) to independence in 1957, making it the first Sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence, and inspiring subsequent African independence movements including Nigeria's.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU), founded in 1963, was primarily established to promote
options: military alliances exclusively directed against Cold War superpowers
the reinstatement of colonial rule in newly independent states
African unity, solidarity, and the eradication of colonialism across the continent
European economic interests in Africa
questions.explanation: The OAU was founded in Addis Ababa in 1963 by newly independent African states to foster continental unity, coordinate cooperation, and support the ongoing struggle against colonialism across Africa.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The system of interlocking alliances before World War I, dividing much of Europe into two major camps, is best exemplified by the
options: Berlin Conference agreements
Warsaw Pact and NATO
Triple Alliance and the Triple Entente
United Nations Charter
questions.explanation: Before World War I, Europe was divided broadly between the Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) and the Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain), a rigid alliance system that helped turn a regional crisis into a general war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The concept of 'total war', closely associated with both World War I and World War II, refers to a conflict in which
options: no modern weapons or technology are used
combat is limited exclusively to naval engagements
entire national economies and civilian populations are mobilised in support of the war effort
fighting is restricted strictly to professional soldiers on clearly defined battlefields
questions.explanation: 'Total war' describes conflicts, like the two World Wars, in which whole societies — industry, civilians, and resources — were mobilised in support of the military effort, blurring the line between combatants and civilians.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Treaty of Versailles imposed on Germany after World War I included a clause, widely resented by Germans, that
options: assigned Germany full responsibility ('war guilt') for causing the war
granted Germany additional overseas colonies
immediately readmitted Germany to full membership of the League of Nations
allowed Germany to keep its full pre-war military strength
questions.explanation: The 'War Guilt Clause' of the Treaty of Versailles placed sole responsibility for the war on Germany, justifying heavy reparations and territorial losses, and fuelling deep German resentment.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party in Germany during the 1930s was significantly aided by
options: widespread economic prosperity across interwar Germany
a lack of any nationalist sentiment in Germany
strong and effective enforcement mechanisms within the League of Nations
severe economic hardship, including hyperinflation and the Great Depression, combined with resentment over Versailles
questions.explanation: Germany's severe economic crises of the 1920s-30s, combined with lingering resentment over the harsh Versailles terms, created fertile conditions that the Nazi Party exploited to gain mass support.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The policy pursued by Britain and France toward Nazi Germany's early territorial expansion in the late 1930s is commonly known as
options: détente
containment
appeasement
isolationism
questions.explanation: Appeasement describes the policy by which Britain and France made concessions to Hitler's territorial demands, such as at the Munich Agreement of 1938, hoping to avoid another major war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Munich Agreement of 1938, a notable example of the appeasement policy, permitted Nazi Germany to annex the
options: Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia
Rhineland region of Germany itself
Alsace-Lorraine region of France
entire territory of Poland
questions.explanation: At the Munich Conference, Britain and France agreed to allow Germany to annex the Sudetenland, a German-speaking region of Czechoslovakia, in a failed attempt to satisfy Hitler's territorial ambitions and avoid war.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The wartime conference at which Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin discussed the post-war reorganisation of Europe, including the division of Germany, was held at
options: San Francisco
Versailles
Yalta
questions.explanation: The 1945 Yalta Conference brought together the leaders of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union to plan the post-war order in Europe, including arrangements for occupied Germany.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The founding charter of the United Nations was formally adopted at a conference held in
options: San Francisco in 1945
Geneva in 1920
Berlin in 1885
Versailles in 1919
questions.explanation: Representatives of fifty nations adopted the United Nations Charter at the San Francisco Conference in 1945, formally establishing the organisation shortly after the end of World War II.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Korean War (1950-1953) is generally regarded as a significant early example of a
options: direct large-scale war between the United States and the Soviet Union
war fought exclusively using nuclear weapons
conflict entirely unrelated to Cold War rivalries
Cold War proxy conflict between forces backed by the capitalist and communist blocs
questions.explanation: The Korean War, pitting a US-led UN coalition against North Korean and Chinese forces, exemplified the pattern of Cold War 'proxy wars' in which the superpowers avoided direct confrontation while backing opposing sides.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely regarded as one of the tensest moments of the Cold War because it
options: resulted in the immediate reunification of Germany
led directly to the founding of the United Nations
brought the United States and the Soviet Union close to direct nuclear confrontation
marked the formal end of the Cold War
questions.explanation: The discovery of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba triggered a tense standoff between the United States and the Soviet Union, widely seen as the moment the world came closest to nuclear war during the Cold War.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 is generally regarded as marking
options: the definitive end of the Cold War era
the beginning of the Cold War
the founding of the League of Nations
the start of World War II
questions.explanation: The formal collapse of the Soviet Union in December 1991 is widely seen as the conclusive end of the decades-long Cold War rivalry between the Eastern and Western blocs.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, each holding veto power, originally comprised the United States, the Soviet Union (later Russia), Britain, France, and
options: Germany
China
India
Japan
questions.explanation: The five permanent, veto-wielding members of the UN Security Council are the United States, Russia (as Soviet successor), Britain, France, and China, reflecting the major Allied powers of World War II.

questions.subject: History
questions.text: The Non-Aligned Movement, which many newly independent African and Asian states (including Nigeria) associated with, emerged as a response to
options: an agreement to support only the League of Nations
a wish to avoid formal alignment with either the Western capitalist bloc or the Soviet-led communist bloc during the Cold War
a formal military alliance directed against the United Nations
a decision to join the Warsaw Pact exclusively
questions.explanation: The Non-Aligned Movement, formed in the early 1960s, allowed newly independent states to pursue independent foreign policies without formally aligning with either Cold War superpower bloc.
